articles.title: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand: Cheslin Kolbe stars with the boot as Springboks level series in Cape Town
articles.summary: South Africa roared back into Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry as returning captain Siya Kolisi marked his comeback with a try in a thrilling 33-26 victory over New Zealand in Cape Town, levelling the four-Test series at 1-1.
articles.body:
Springboks strike back in Cape Town to level Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series with All Blacks; four-Test battle moves to Johannesburg for third clash on September 5; watch every minute of New Zealand's tour of South Africa exclusively live on Sky Sports

South Africa roared back into Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry as returning captain Siya Kolisi marked his comeback with a try in a thrilling 33-26 victory over New Zealand in Cape Town, levelling the four-Test series at 1-1.

The sides shared seven tries, with Jesse Kriel, Damian de Allende and Kolisi crossing for the Springboks, either side of scores from Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie and Leroy Carter. But Cheslin Kolbe's 18 points from the tee ultimately proved decisive.

All Blacks captain Ardie Savea added a late fourth try for New Zealand - his 33rd in Test rugby - as the visitors finished with four tries to South Africa's three, but they were unable to overcome Kolbe's flawless accuracy.

Savea had predicted before kick-off that New Zealand would face a "wounded beast", and South Africa delivered an immediate response. Kriel crossed inside the opening two minutes, only for Roigard to hit back midway through a breathless opening quarter.

Kolbe's first penalty and de Allende's try either side of the 20-minute mark reasserted South African control. McKenzie's converted score kept the All Blacks within touching distance, but Kolisi crashed over on the stroke of half-time to send the hosts into the break with a 24-14 lead.

The 32-year-old's boot then tightened South Africa's grip after the break, with two penalties in three minutes stretching the lead beyond two scores. Carter's unconverted try briefly gave the All Blacks hope, but the wing's fourth penalty effectively settled the contest.

"We know last week we let it slip," said Kolbe, who was named player of the match. "We could feel the mood from the South Africa fans. We just wanted to do the jersey proud, our families proud.

"You need to take every point given to you. That's Test match rugby. We stuck to the plan to take the points on offer."

Savea admitted the All Blacks had paid for their slow start.

"We kind of let the Springboks get ahead in the first two minutes and we were chasing the game," said the New Zealand captain. "We stuck in there but we came up short. It's a tough pill to swallow.

"We lost the battle tonight but we haven't lost the war. We'll get back on the horse this week and go again."

The New Zealand captain also paid tribute to Pieter-Steph du Toit, who won his 100th cap, and Ox Nche, who won his 50th, for their respective milestones.

"It's been a massive week," Kolisi said. "Last week we didn't take our opportunities but this week we did. Coach Rassie [Erasmus] always reminds us that this is not just about us, it's about all of South Africa. We knew that the mood was down this past week.

"Next week is going to be big. Some of us are playing for the first time in Soweto. It's hard playing them once. Playing them four times in a row is incredibly difficult."

Defeat would have handed South Africa successive home losses for the first time since 2015, but Erasmus' side instead travel to Johannesburg with momentum restored.

South Africa shut out pre-match disruption to level series

South Africa's preparations were anything but settled in the build-up to the game.

Erasmus made five changes to the team he had originally named, with Handre Pollard and Kurt-Lee Arendse withdrawing on Friday. That prompted the head coach to recall Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu at fly-half, just a week after dropping him, while Kolbe was brought into the starting XV on the wing.

There was another late twist an hour before kick-off when Deon Fourie, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit were promoted to the starting front row. Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche and Wilco Louw consequently dropped to the bench, with no reason given for the last-minute reshuffle.

On a more positive note, Kolisi returned to captain the side after missing the opening Test, while two-time World Rugby Player of the Year Du Toit celebrated his 100th Test cap.

New Zealand made three changes from their victory at Ellis Park, with winger Leroy Carter replacing Josh Moorby, while George Bower and Tupou Vaa'i came into the pack for Ethan de Groot and Josh Lord, who were both ruled out with concussion. Ruben Love retained the fly-half jersey, while Beauden Barrett was again left out of the matchday 23.

The All Blacks' five-try, 33-16 victory in Johannesburg had lifted them above the world champions to the top of the world rankings, giving Dave Rennie's side the early advantage in the first full Test series between the nations in three decades.

But the response South Africa demanded duly arrived in Cape Town. The Springboks levelled the series at 1-1 and extended a formidable home record that has seen them lose just one series on South African soil in the past 30 years.

The tour, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, is New Zealand's first full visit to South Africa since 1996. The All Blacks arrived in Cape Town unbeaten on the trip, having defeated the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls before narrowly escaping with victory over the Lions in a midweek clash in Johannesburg.

The series now moves to FNB Stadium for the third Test on September 5, before concluding with a historic first meeting on American soil at Baltimore's M&T Bank Stadium on September 12.

articles.title: Super League: St Helens 6-34 Leeds Rhinos - Rhinos go back top
articles.summary: Leeds Rhinos go back to the top of the Super League standings on points difference with a rare and comprehensive away win at St Helens.
articles.body:
Tries: Hankinson, Smith, Newman, Hall, Handley, Croft Goals: Connor 5

Leeds Rhinos moved back to the top of Super League on points difference with a rare and comprehensive away win at St Helens.

The Rhinos' first win at Saints since March 2023 means they will secure their first League Leaders' Shield for 11 years if they beat second-placed Wigan in a decider for the trophy next Saturday.

Cameron Smith scored the pick of the Rhinos' six tries on the night with a stunning individual effort as they raced into a commanding 18-point lead at the break.

Defeat for St Helens signals a damaging blow to their hopes of making this season's play-offs, failing to capitalise on Hull KR's heavy defeat last night by Wigan , staying two points below the sixth-placed Robins with two games remaining.

Huddersfield upset Leigh with five-try win

Catalans beat Cas in game halted by power outage

After an impeccably observed minute's silence in honour of the late Sir Billy Boston by everyone inside the Brewdog Stadium, an incisive dash and short ball from Jake Connor allowed Chris Hankinson to crash over from close range to break the deadlock.

Leeds momentarily thought they had scored a second try in two minutes as Cooper Jenkins went over under the sticks but Brodie Croft was penalised for a forward pass when attempting to knock the ball backwards.

While down to 12 men because of Daniel Suluka-Fifita's hit on Presley Cassell off the ball, Saints thought they were over but Tristan Sailor's lofted pass to Deon Cross was spotted to be forward as the winger dived in at the left corner.

Second-rower Smith then broke a tackle from Suluka-Fifita, back on the field, and gave the Saints backline a clean set of heels before getting down low to finish off an outstanding individual score.

The match was effectively taken away from Saints when slick hands from Connor set up Ash Handley who in turn found Harry Newman to dive over unopposed as Connor slotted the extras to give Leeds an 18-point lead at the break.

Tom Holroyd had a try disallowed a minute after half-time, unable to ground the ball before knocking on under pressure from Saints full-back Sailor.

Leeds did get their fourth try soon after though when Jack Bird's beautiful backhanded offload freed up Ryan Hall to dot down his 357th career try.

Saints were on the board when Jack Welsby's line break saw him race clear of Leeds' midfield and full-back Lachie Miller for the match's second excellent individual try.

But that proved to be just brief respite as Handley got on the scoresheet, latching on to a grubber kick from Connor, and another grubber from Connor found his half-back partner Croft, via the upright, for his 28th Super League try of the season.

Connor missed a penalty late on, striking the post, but his kicking game continues to impress with Leeds looking strong going into the upcoming play-offs.

Saints, meanwhile, will have to beat Leigh and Hull KR in their final two matches if they are to avoid missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time.

Leeds Rhinos coach Brad Arthur told BBC Radio Leeds:

"I thought both our starts to the first half and the second half were pretty good. We did it with a good control.

"We had to stay composed and that was a good test for us. We had players all over the shop the last 15 minutes but they still had a pride in their defence which has been a bit questionable at times this season.

"If we can withstand the pressure for three, four sets, which we're going to have to do against Wigan next week, it can take a bit of confidence out of your opposition.

"We're up against a really good team who have been at the top of their game for a long, long time. So we're excited, we've done the work, now we've got to be confident."

St Helens: Sailor; Douglas, MacDonald, Welsby, Cross; Robertson, Lomax; Suluka-Fifita, Shorrocks, Klemmer, Davies, Wright, Host.

Interchanges: Walmsley, Humphreys, Keeley, Evans.

Leeds: Miller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell.

Interchanges: Holroyd, Smith, Levi, Lodge.

articles.title: Super League: Huddersfield Giants 30-18 Hull KR
articles.summary: Huddersfield Giants score five tries to upset in-form Leigh and keep the Leopards waiting to secure their place in the Super League play-offs.
articles.body:
Tries: Rushton, Milne, Evalds, Geyer 2 Goals: Flanagan 5

Tries: Trout, Hanley, Mulhern Goals: Cook 3

Huddersfield Giants scored five tries to upset in-form Leigh and keep the Leopards waiting to secure their place in the Super League play-offs.

Leigh scored the night's first try through Owen Trout but tries from Harry Rushton and Taane Milne helped put Huddersfield 14-6 ahead at half-time.

Niall Evalds extended the lead after the break before Leigh's Umyla Hanley and Huddersfield's Cole Geyer exchanged tries as the Giants remained ahead.

Robbie Mulhern's try kept Leigh alive with 11 minutes to play but Geyer's second score with six minutes remaining sealed an impressive victory for Huddersfield.

Victory for Huddersfield was their seventh of the season, with five of those victories coming in their past six matches, and moved them up to 12th in the table and above York ahead of their trip to Toulouse.

Leigh arrived having won eight of their past nine games and victory would have secured their place in the top six.

They remain fifth and are still well-placed to reach the play-offs with two games remaining after St Helens, in seventh, lost at home to Leeds.

The visitors scored the opening try after nine minutes as Trout claimed an up-and-under and reached out to score.

But Huddersfield responded with 14 points in 10 minutes before half-time.

Rushton barged over before George Flanagan kicked a penalty from in front of the posts and then Tui Lolohea's high kick was spilled by Leigh's Innes Senior and the ball fell for Milne to run in.

Leeds go back top with thumping win at St Helens

Catalans beat Tigers after delay for power outage

Leading 14-6 at the start of the second half, Zac Woolford broke from dummy half and found Evalds to score Huddersfield's third try.

Needing a response, Leigh released Josh Charnley up the right wing and sent Hanley over on his 100th Super League appearance.

But Huddersfield forced a goal-line drop-out that was taken short, Giants claimed the kick and they drove towards the line before Woolford grubbered in-goal for Geyer to dot down.

Leigh kept themselves alive again as they reclaimed the restart, were immediately in behind the defence and sent Mulhern over from the next play.

But they soon knocked on to give Huddersfield field position and Geyer found a gap to slide in for his second try to seal the game.

Leigh head coach Adrian Lam told BBC Radio Manchester:

"It was hard to watch and nothing like we've been over the past four months.

"I thought Huddersfield were great, they were very physical and on point and we knew we were going to come here and have a tough game.

"We knew we needed to be sharp with high completions and minimum errors and we just came out of that really badly and it's the worst we've played over the last three-four months."

Huddersfield: Evalds; Milne, Jagger, Halsall, Zenon; Lolohea, Clune; Powell, Woolford, King, Hewitt, Cozza, Rushton

Interchanges: Rogers, Flanagan, Billington, Geyer

Leigh: O'Brien; Senior, Badrock, Hanley, Charnley; Cook, Lam; Ofahengaue, Horne, Mulhern, Hughes, Trout, Liu

Interchanges: Brogan, Ashworth, Alick-Wiencke, Ipape

articles.title: Museu Paulo Setúbal em Tatuí inicia obras de recuperação estrutural | G1
articles.standfirst: O prédio, construído em 1920, está fechado para visitação desde maio do ano passado. Avaliações feitas no imóvel identificaram fissuras e trincas.
articles.summary: O Museu Histórico Paulo Setúbal iniciou obras de R$ 831 mil para corrigir fissuras no prédio de 1920, com previsão de reabertura para 2027.
articles.body:
Museu Histórico Paulo Setúbal, em Tatuí (SP), passa por obras de revitalização — Foto: Prefeitura de Tatuí/Divulgação

O Museu Histórico “Paulo Setúbal”, em Tatuí (SP), começou a passar por obras de adequação estrutural na segunda-feira (24). O prédio, construído em 1920, está fechado para visitação desde maio do ano passado.

A intervenção foi contratada por R$ 831 mil e é executada por uma empresa de Indaiatuba (SP). A obra recebe apoio financeiro da família Setúbal.

Segundo a prefeitura, o projeto foi elaborado a partir de estudos e pareceres técnicos de engenharia e aprovado por unanimidade pelo Conselho Municipal de Defesa do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico de Tatuí (Condephat).

As avaliações realizadas no imóvel identificaram fissuras e trincas associadas ao recalque das fundações ao longo dos anos . Para solucionar os problemas estruturais e adequar o prédio às normas de segurança, o projeto prevê três principais intervenções:

Reforço das fundações com a instalação de estacas do tipo Mega;

Adequação do Sistema de Proteção contra Descargas Atmosféricas (SPDA);

Regularização e modernização do sistema de combate a incêndios.

De acordo com a administração municipal, as medidas têm como objetivo aumentar a segurança do prédio, proteger o acervo histórico e permitir a retomada das atividades culturais e educativas no local.

O museu está fechado ao público desde 26 de maio de 2025, quando começaram os estudos, avaliações e procedimentos preparatórios para a obra.

Museu Histórico Paulo Setúbal, em Tatuí, entra em obras de recuperação estrutural — Foto: Reprodução

A prefeitura informou que pretende concluir a recuperação estrutural e reabrir o prédio durante o período de comemorações do Bicentenário de Tatuí, que se estende até 10 de agosto de 2027.

Enquanto o museu permanece fechado, os serviços administrativos e as ações relacionadas ao acervo e à preservação da instituição continuam.

As atividades educativas e culturais foram transferidas para o Complexo Cultural de Memória, que reúne o Museu da Imagem e do Som (MIS) Tatuí e para o Memorial do Rugby 1928.

A execução da obra ocorre após estudos técnicos, sondagem do solo, elaboração do projeto estrutural, análise pelos órgãos competentes e articulação para a obtenção dos recursos.

O museu também deverá receber um novo projeto expográfico, desenvolvido com apoio do Instituto Fundação Itaú.

Segundo a prefeitura, a proposta é renovar a apresentação do acervo e ampliar as possibilidades de interação do público com a história de Tatuí e com o patrimônio preservado pela instituição.

O projeto deverá respeitar o plano museológico criado em 2009.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Aviões da Embraer voam próximo a estádio durante jogo de rúgbi | G1
articles.standfirst: Apresentação das aeronaves da Airlink aconteceu durante partida entre África do Sul e Nova Zelândia neste sábado (29).
articles.summary: Apresentação das aeronaves da Airlink aconteceu durante partida entre África do Sul e Nova Zelândia neste sábado (29).
articles.body:
Dois aviões E195-E2 da Embraer , com sede em São José dos Campos , no interior de São Paulo, fizeram um voo rasante em cima do DHL Stadium, na Cidade do Cabo, na África do Sul, durante uma partida de rúgbi neste sábado (29).

A partida foi entre África do Sul e Nova Zelândia e terminou com a vitória dos sul-africanos por 33 a 26.

Pelas imagens divulgadas pelo Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, é possível ver o momento em que as duas aeronaves sobrevoam o estádio antes da partida. Em seguida, fogos coloridos são ativados.

Nas redes sociais, a Embraer já havia divulgado uma ação com a companhia sul-africana Airlink, na passagem dos aviões no estádio Ellis Park, também na África do Sul.

Aviões da Embraer sobrevoam bem próximo a estádio na África do Sul — Foto: Rugby's Greatest Rivalry

articles.title: Ulster Rugby: 'Small steps' for Joe Schmidt at province says Rory Best
articles.summary: Rory Best says Joe Schmidt's new role with Ulster is a case of "small steps" as the province seek to use the former Ireland coach's expertise to build a platform for long-term success.
articles.body:
Rory Best says Joe Schmidt's new role with Ulster is a case of "small steps" as the province seek to use the former Ireland coach's expertise to build a platform for long-term success.

Schmidt was appointed Ulster's coach development adviser last month after ending his two-year stint as Australia boss, a newly created role focused on the province's coaching pathway.

The 60-year-old is one of Ireland's most successful coaches having led the national team to three Six Nations titles - including the 2018 Grand Slam - during a six-year spell and Leinster to two European Cups.

"I don't want to just be successful this season or in a year or two, it has to be a continuous process and to do that we need continuity of what's coming behind it and that's why Joe is here," said Ulster general manager Rory Best, who was appointed Ireland captain by Schmidt in 2016.

"Joe was the best coach I worked under as a head coach. Since then, he's went on, he's coached the All Blacks, Australia. He's across the New Zealand underage system, the Australian underage system, from his time in Leinster the Irish underage system.

"So to bring all the best practices together, ultimately what you want to do is to create a conveyor belt. The lift it gives everyone around the place is brilliant. We're delighted to have him.

"Obviously the next step is to get him head to toe in Ulster gear, but it's small steps."

Schmidt was present at an open training session for Ulster's senior men's team in Banbridge on Friday as Murphy's side ramp up preparations for the 2026-27 season.

Murphy - who worked alongside the Kiwi at Leinster and Ireland - said it was a "genius idea" by Best to get Schmidt involved.

"Myself and Joe go back a long time. Besty, I thought it was a genius idea bringing him over," he said.

"He's helping through the pathway and having a look at that area and making sure we have a supply of players to feed this Ulster senior team.

"He's here today to have a look at training and we'd be crazy not to use a person like that in relation in giving us a bit of feedback about how we go about our business."

Murphy is in the process of reintegrating Ulster's cohort of Ireland internationals back into training after their Nations Championship exertions in July.

A promising 2025-26 season ended in disappointing fashion for Ulster as they missed out on Investec Champions Cup qualification after finishing ninth in the United Rugby Championship and losing the Challenge Cup final to Montpellier.

Ulster face Edinburgh and Ospreys in pre-season friendlies before beginning their URC campaign against the former in Belfast on 25 September.

During a busy summer of squad additions and departures, Ulster signed the likes of forwards Eli Snyman, Ben Donnell and Keynan Knox and backs Chay Mullins, Matthew Devine and Jamie Benson, while losing key players such as Werner Kok and Angus Bell.

"I think our squad depth has improved, especially in key positions," said Murphy, who is entering his third full season in charge.

"Ben Donnell can play in back row and second row, Eli in the second row gives us more experience in that area. Two tight-heads knocking around in Keynan Knox and Eduardo Bello creates pressure and competition for places which is really positive.

"Tom O'Toole, Scotty Wilson and Tom McAllister were there last year, those lads have to fight it out now to get themselves on the pitch, which is great.

"Our two half-backs that have come in, Matty Devine and young Benson, they've both fitted in really well and upped the level of competition to get your name on the sheet, so that's been really positive."

images.caption: Image caption, Rory Best (right) says the arrival of former Ireland boss Joe Schmidt (left) has given Ulster a "lift"
Image caption, Irish-qualified back-three player Chay Mullins is one of several new faces in the Ulster squad

articles.title: South Africa 33-26 New Zealand: Springboks level 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series
articles.summary: World champions South Africa deliver a powerful first-half performance as they edge past New Zealand and level 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1.
articles.body:
'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series - second Test

Tries: Kriel, De Allende, Kolisi Cons: Kolbe 3 Pens: Kolbe 4

Tries: Roigard, McKenzie, Carter, Savea Cons: Love 3

World champions South Africa delivered a powerful first-half performance as they edged past New Zealand and levelled 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series at 1-1 with two Tests to play.

The All Blacks travelled to Cape Town knowing a win would write them into the history books as the first New Zealand team to win back-to-back Tests in South Africa since the 'Incomparables' of 1996.

But South Africa dominated the basics and showed a more clinical edge this week, even though the lively All Blacks again outscored them on the try count by four to three.

New Zealand's fightback ultimately came too late, captain Ardie Savea barging over on 77 minutes to get the game within a score, but on the All Blacks' final attack Boks replacement Cameron Hanekom won a superb turnover that settled the nervy closing stages.

As he did last week, Springboks wing Cheslin Kolbe took on the kicking duties over fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, notching up 18 points in a player-of-the-match performance.

The first series in 30 years between these two mighty rugby nations is shaping into an epic, with the third Test back at altitude in Soweto, Johannesburg next Saturday.

The Springbok team that took the field at the Cape Town Stadium was markedly different to the one originally named by head coach Rassie Erasmus on Monday .

Fly-half Handre Pollard was fit and then injured and withdrawn in the week, while Kolbe was injured and then fit and eventually named on the wing.

On top of that, Erasmus switched around his whole front row in the hours before kick-off, with the starting trio dropping to the bench and vice-versa.

It meant there were five changes in all from the matchday squad announced on Monday and surely would have had the New Zealand management thumbing through the regulations of the tour agreement.

Despite producing a famous rearguard effort in the first-Test victory at Ellis Park, New Zealand boss Dave Rennie warned in the week his side would need to "go deeper" to cope with the inevitable Springbok backlash.

That South African onslaught came from the off.

Hooker Deon Fourie, at nearly 40 the oldest Springbok in history, found his target in the line-out, the South African maul powered into the 22, and lightning fast ball led to centre Jesse Kriel crashing over.

Kolbe added the extras as the world champions made the dream start.

But despite the fast start from the hosts, New Zealand grew into the contest, with referee Angus Gardner, himself a late call-up in place of Nika Amashukeli, presiding over a fast and fluent game.

Damian McKenzie made a clean break which almost put in Will Jordan, and while the Boks killed the ball from the ensuing breakdown, Eben Etzebeth got up to spoil New Zealand's five-metre line-out.

Despite their set-piece issues, the All Blacks came again. Intricate handling freed Jordan, who used his pace and strength to escape down the right and link with the outstanding Cam Roigard. Ruben Love levelled the scores from bang in front.

That score lit a fire in the Springboks, with Kolbe kicking a penalty and Damian de Allende barrelling over after another imposing maul as South Africa showed far more ruthlessness compared to a week ago.

With the Springboks dominating in the basics, the crowd in Cape Town smelt blood as the lead stretched to 17-7.

But with ball in hand, Rennie's crop are reminiscent of the great All Blacks side of old. Savea burst forward from a line-out, and perfect passing gave McKenzie a walk-in.

At 17-14 edging towards half-time the contest was in the balance, before a match-defining sequence just before the interval.

Kolbe forced a five-metre scrum, before which Erasmus brought on two of his strongest scrummagers in Malcolm Marx and Ox Nche, who immediately won a penalty.

From there, another scrum, another penalty advantage, and with the All Blacks back-pedalling captain Siya Kolisi crashed over for South Africa's third try and a 10-point lead after a pulsating first 40.

New Zealand needed to score first in the second half, and they didn't, losing the ball when in Bok territory and then giving away a soft penalty which Kolbe kicked.

The All Blacks were on the ropes, Marx won a breakdown penalty, and Kolbe stretched the lead to 16 points with half an hour to go.

With the second half lacking the fireworks of the first, the All Blacks backs – led by Roigard - desperately tried to drag New Zealand back into the match.

After another McKenzie break led to nothing, some more beautiful handling resulted in Leroy Carter scampering into the left corner, a fabulous finish.

More excellent attacking play released Jordan down the right, and the recycled ball found skipper Savea, who crashed over to cut the gap to seven points with two minutes remaining.

But the Springboks held on, despite lock Lood de Jager being sent to the sin-bin for a high tackle.

Fittingly, it was a breakdown penalty that settled the game, with Hanekom winning the crucial turnover in an area South Africa dominated.

The All Blacks' impressive win in the first Test had temporarily shot them above South Africa in the world rankings, something Erasmus urged his side to rectify.

That they did, and with normal service resumed in the eyes of the Springboks supporters, South Africa travel back to the Highveld with the momentum.

But the All Blacks have played some wonderful rugby in the first two Tests, and will still believe they can join the legends of 1996.

The eyes of the rugby world now turn to Soweto.

articles.title: Super League: Wakefield Trinity 28-12 York Knights - hosts secure play-off spot
articles.summary: Second-half tries by Jayden Myers, Max Jowitt and Lachlan Walmsley help Wakefield Trinity beat York Knights to move fourth in Super League.
articles.body:
Tries: Hall, Walmsley 2, Myers, Jowitt Goals: Jowitt 4

Tries: Jones-Bishop, Va'a Goals: Bennison 2

Second-half tries by Jayden Myers, Max Jowitt and Lachlan Walmsley helped Wakefield Trinity beat York Knights at the DIY Kitchens Stadium to secure a place in the Super League play-offs.

Corey Hall had put the hosts in front against the second-bottom side, although former Trinity player Ben Jones-Bishop reduced York's deficit to two points before Walmsley scored as Trinity took a six-point lead into the break.

Xavier Va'a's rampaging run and Jon Bennison's conversion drew York level early in the second half, but Myers went over from Mike McMeeken's pass and Jon Bennison's attempted pass went straight to full-back Jowitt, who scored and set up Walmsley for the final try six minutes later.

The win ended Trinity's three-match losing run as they moved two points clear in fourth place and six points above St Helens, who are seventh.

Their prospects of home advantage in an eliminator could hinge on their final home game of the regular season next Saturday against Warrington Wolves, who are four points above them and still within reach of the top two following their win at Hull FC .

York have now lost four games in a row but they remain level on points in the table with fourth-bottom Hull.

Leeds go back top with thumping win at St Helens

Huddersfield upset Leigh with five-try win

Trinity had threatened a top-two finish during a seven-match winning run in June and August, but defeats by Wigan Warriors, St Helens and Leeds Rhinos had ended those ambitions and head coach Daryl Powell will not have been entirely convinced by their display against York, who started the evening 18 points behind them.

After a minute's silence in honour of the late Sir Billy Boston, Powell's side made a bright start, their ample pressure paying off when Jack Sinfield's clever low kick allowed centre Hall to score his fourth try of the season.

The visitors looked increasingly confident after falling behind and hit back through Jones-Bishop in the right-hand corner, marking the back's first appearance since a home defeat by Wakefield on 27 March as part of an injury-hindered season.

Jowitt missed his conversion after Walmsley swiftly scored from Hall's ball, but McMeeken looked to have extended Trinity's lead early in the second half, only for the try to be disallowed when a video review ruled that Jowitt had impeded Scott Galeano.

Samoan prop Va'a duly barged through at the other end for York's second try, Bennison adding the points to put the contest in the balance before Ky Rodwell won a penalty that was kicked by Jowitt to put Trinity back in front.

That lead had lasted three minutes by the time Bennison's penalty restored parity, with York capitalising when Tyson Smoothy committed a high tackle on fellow replacement Ata Hingano.

Wakefield's run of three tries in 10 minutes began with McMeeken's masterful delivery to Myers, and Jowitt then increased the margin in far more fortuitous fashion.

Bennison looked disconsolate after throwing a pass inside to no-one, allowing Jowitt to score and all but end York's hopes of a surprise result in a week when the club announced a deal had been struck to sell a majority stake to new investors.

Walmsley's second try and Jowitt's third successful conversion with four minutes remaining perhaps made the scoreline harsh on York, who are two points above Bradford Bulls with the bottom side visiting Toulouse Olympique on Saturday evening.

York host Bradford in their final fixture on 10 September, coming after a trip to eighth-placed Catalans Dragons in their closing away game next Saturday.

Wakefield prop Mike McMeeken told BBC Sport:

"The main [requirement] was patience. It took us 60 or 70 minutes to break York down. We knew it was going to need an 80-minute performance.

"[Inclement] conditions like this are perfect for us to learn because if we want to get to the Grand Final come October at Old Trafford it will be a wet Saturday night like this.

"We'd like to get a home [eliminator] - that would be ideal. We were pushing for the top two, but now it's just about getting that confidence back. This helps."

York Knights head coach Mark Applegarth told BBC Radio York:

"First, congratulations to Wakefield. We wish them all the best in the play-offs and they're a quality team.

"It was a really tight game. We spoke at half-time about showing more urgency on the floor, generating more tempo, getting more field position and investing more energy in the first two tackles, to slow the rucks down so Wakefield couldn't roll us as easily.

"We told our lads to chance their arm a bit and go for glory in that last 20, so that's probably why we ended up a little more sloppy."

articles.title: Super League: Hull FC 14-16 Warrington Wolves - Wire hold off fightback for sixth straight win
articles.summary: Warrington hold off a spirited late Hull FC fightback to secure their sixth successive win and keep a top-two finish in Super League in sight.
articles.body:
Tries: Hayes, Ashton, Thewlis Goals: Williams 2

Warrington Wolves held off a spirited late Hull FC fightback to secure their sixth successive win and retain their hopes of a top-two finish in Super League.

With the scores tied at 2-2 heading into the final five minutes of the first half, errors in defence allowed the away side to score back-to-back tries through Leon Hayes and Matty Ashton.

Josh Thewlis extended Wire's lead with the home side down to 12 men after Ligi Sao was sin-binned for a high shot on Ashton.

Ethan O'Neill crossed for the home side's first try and Tom Briscoe, making his final home appearance for Hull before retiring, quickly got a second to cut Warrington's lead to just two points, but the third-placed visitors held out to move two points behind Leeds Rhinos and Wigan Warriors.

The tone for what was at times an attritional encounter played in wet conditions in East Yorkshire was set in the opening minute when the home side had James Batchelor sin-binned for a tackle on Arron Lindop, who subsequently failed a head injury assessment.

Warrington captain George Williams kicked the away side into the lead after 18 minutes before Aidan Sezer made it 2-2 from a Hull penalty shortly afterwards.

It looked like that was how the half would end but the home side, who have now lost 18 of their 25 Super League matches this year, then produced two errors under high kicks in three minutes that were both punished by Sam Burgess' men as Hayes and Ashton went over.

Thewlis' score ten minutes into the second half seemed to have put the game out of reach of Hull before the home side surprisingly rallied with 15 minutes to go.

O'Neill went over on Hull's left before the retiring Briscoe scored the 233rd try of his illustrious career.

The Black and Whites pushed for another score but Warrington held out, while the home side were perhaps lucky to end the game with 13 men on the field with Sao involved in further incidents after his sin-binning.

The Wolves head to fourth-placed Wakefield next Saturday, with Hull travelling to Toulouse Olympique on Friday.

articles.title: Una imagen que asusta: dos aviones pasan rozando un estadio de Sudáfrica antes del partido de rugby entre los Springbooks y los All Blacks
articles.standfirst: Era una maniobra de exhibición que estaba planeada
articles.summary: Era una maniobra de exhibición que estaba planeada
articles.body: Este sábado, el DHL Stadium de Ciudad del Cabo fue escenario de un imponente sobrevuelo en paralelo protagonizado por dos aviones Embraer de la aerolínea Airlink, instantes antes de que diera comienzo el esperado enfrentamiento entre los Springboks sudafricanos y los All Blacks neozelandeses que contaba con 55.000 espectadores en su interior. Las imágenes difundidas en redes sociales captan el momento en que ambas aeronaves avanzaban casi a la par y rozaban la estructura del recinto a escasa altitud antes de remontar el vuelo. La maniobra, que generó un gran impacto visual por la sensación de proximidad, formaba parte del show previo al choque. Horas antes, la propia compañía —patrocinadora aérea oficial de la denominada Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry 2026— había confirmado el pase. Para la exhibición se emplearon un Embraer E190 (matrícula ZS-YAE), luciendo los colores verdes de la escuadra sudafricana, y un Embraer E195 (ZS-YDE), vestido con el característico tono negro de los neozelandeses, ambos con diseños especiales dedicados a esta histórica pugna deportiva. No es la primera vez que la pareja de aviones realiza esta exhibición: el pasado 22 de agosto ya completaron un pase idéntico sobre el Ellis Park de Johannesburgo en el primer test de la serie. Sin embargo, la brevedad de la distancia al suelo registrada este sábado ha reavivado el debate entre aviadores y entusiastas del sector. Aunque la regulación aérea en Sudáfrica fija unos márgenes mínimos de altitud al sobrevolar eventos multitudinarios, la norma contempla excepciones para maniobras especiales si cuentan con el visto bueno de la autoridad competente. De momento, Airlink no ha detallado cuál era el techo de vuelo fijado en el permiso, ni la Autoridad de Aviación Civil de Sudáfrica (SACAA) se ha pronunciado al respecto. Con el único respaldo de las grabaciones de los aficionados, resulta imposible precisar si los pilotos se desviaron o no de los límites autorizados.

articles.title: Stella Orrin: A French mum, 'no good player' dad and Welsh tears on debut
articles.summary: Rising rugby star Stella Orrin reflects on her pride at making her senior Wales debut as she targets a first cap in the autumn internationals.
articles.body:
When Stella Orrin was told she had made her first senior matchday squad, there were so many tears that Wales head coach Sean Lynn had to call her back just to make sure she got the message.

There was a similar outburst of emotion when Orrin stood for the national anthem before making her debut off the bench in Wales' victory over the Barbarians in June.

"It's the best day of my life so far," said the 20-year-old prop.

"I'm so proud. I've been working towards putting that jersey on for such a long time and it really means a lot to me.

"I remember when Lynny told me. Before the team is announced he has a one-to-one with you. I thought it was going to be bad news... I was just so emotional that I couldn't take anything in. I just burst into tears."

Neumann back in Wales' extended WXV training squad

Could study into head injuries change women's rugby?

The only thing that could have topped Orrin's Twickenham outing was if it had been a capped Test match, but that is something the young tight-head could achieve this autumn when Wales take on South Africa, USA and Japan in the WXV Global Series.

While Orrin admits she would burst with pride at the prospect, the former Wales Under-18s and Under-21s prop is biding her time.

"I really trust the coaches and the girls that are around me, my time will come," she said.

"I'm in no rush to get there, but if I could it would be great.

"I'm so proud to be Welsh. It's the country that welcomed my mother from France, it's the country that I get to tell all my friends about when I go to university in Bristol."

Like most internationals, Orrin has her family to thank for their support, with her rugby-playing dad the reason she started playing the game aged 13.

"He was no good," Orrin says in fits of laughter. "I say no good, he just played social rugby in the valleys.

"I started playing the cello and rugby because I really wanted to be like him. He's my idol.

"My parents come to every game and my dad buys tickets for all of our fixtures before I've even been picked.

"For all the Six Nations games when I was travelling reserve, all my family came. They were still so proud that I was running my tempos on the side."

Orrin is currently being put through her paces during pre-season with Wales, before Lynn narrows his WXV training squad down before their opener against South Africa on 18 September.

It is Orrin's second year training with the senior squad and credits players such as Donna Rose and Gwen Crabb in helping her step up from age-grade rugby.

"All the girls have to be fair. It's quite surreal, especially last year when I came in for my first time," said Orrin.

"These are people that you see on the telly and you're all like 'ooh it's Jaz Joyce and Lisa Neumann'.

"But then you come in and you find out that they're not just great players, they're really incredible people."

articles.title: Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry schedule, results, kick-off times and how to watch South Africa vs New Zealand
articles.summary: Everything you need to know as the Springboks and All Blacks meet in a new series
articles.body:
Old foes South Africa and New Zealand collide in a new series in the first "Rugby's Greatest Rivalry" tour.

The Springboks and All Blacks have reached a reciprocal touring agreement that will see the pair clash in a number of Tests every four years.

The first edition sees Dave Rennie's side head for South African soil to take on four United Rugby Championship sides alongside a quartet of clashes with Rassie Erasmus's world champions.

The fourth of those fixtures, which brings together the World Cup finalists from three years ago, will take place in Baltimore on the east coast of the United States.

Rugby's Greatest Rivalry schedule (all times BST)

5 September: South Africa vs New Zealand (4.10pm, Johannesburg) THIRD TEST

12 September: South Africa vs New Zealand (10pm, Baltimore) FOURTH TEST

Viewers in the United Kingdom can watch the series live on Sky Sports, which has struck a deal for the broadcasting rights. In South Africa, coverage available via SuperSport.

articles.title: El rugby que sobrevivió a los Andes
articles.standfirst: Antonio de Castro, psicólogo deportivo del Cisneros, analiza las claves de un deporte donde la unión hace la fuerza
articles.summary: Antonio de Castro, psicólogo deportivo del Cisneros, analiza las claves de un deporte donde la unión hace la fuerza
articles.body: "Empezaron a organizarse desde el minuto uno porque ya estaban organizados antes de estrellarse". Así explica Antonio de Castro, psicólogo deportivo del Cisneros la tragedia de octubre de 1972. En mitad de los Andes, un accidente de avión deja a un grupo de jóvenes aislados del mundo. Rodeados de nieve y enfrentados a condiciones extremas, descubren que sobrevivir ya no depende de ninguno de ellos por separado. Muchos son jugadores del Old Christians Club, un equipo de rugby uruguayo que se dirigía hacia Chile para disputar un partido. Están acostumbrados a avanzar juntos, a confiar en el compañero y a entender que, cuando uno cae, otro ocupa su lugar. Fuera del campo, aquella idea adquirió una dimensión inimaginable: el equipo como supervivencia. Más de medio siglo después y a miles de kilómetros de la cordillera andina, el rugby sigue construyéndose alrededor de la palabra equipo. Aquella tragedia llevó hasta el extremo unos valores que forman parte de la esencia de este deporte. Para Antonio de Castro, la explicación de lo ocurrido en los Andes comienza precisamente antes del accidente. Antes del frío, del hambre y de los 72 días atrapados en la montaña. Comienza cuando aquellos jóvenes todavía eran simplemente compañeros de rugby. "Para mí, la clave de por qué pudieron sobrevivir es que eran un equipo y, segundo que eran un equipo de rugby". Hoy, lejos de aquel escenario límite, la psicología ha pedido paso para ocupar un lugar cada vez más importante dentro y fuera del terreno de juego. En medio de una situación en la que cualquier estructura conocida había desaparecido, ellos conservaron una: la del equipo. Repartieron funciones, asumieron responsabilidades y redujeron un problema gigantesco a pequeños objetivos. Conseguir agua. Acondicionar el fuselaje. Atender a los heridos. Preparar una expedición. Sobrevivir una noche más. Antonio lo explica con un concepto muy visual: “Funcionaron como una mente colmena”. Según relata el psicólogo, apenas necesitaron tres minutos para comenzar a organizarse tras el impacto. Roberto Canessa y Gustavo Zerbino, estudiantes de Medicina, comenzaron a atender a los heridos; Marcelo Pérez del Castillo, capitán del equipo, asumió la organización del grupo. “Empezaron a organizarse desde el minuto uno porque ya estaban organizados antes de estrellarse”, explica. Ahí encuentra una de las particularidades del rugby. En otros deportes, las grandes estrellas pueden terminar convirtiéndose en la principal referencia del equipo. En rugby, sostiene Antonio, la individualidad pierde sentido cuando deja de estar al servicio del colectivo. "Cuando el yo se convierte en nosotros", resume recurriendo a una frase de Gustavo Zerbino. "El rugby es uno de los pocos deportes en los que, si de verdad no eres un equipo, no tienes nada que hacer. Aquí no valen ni las individualidades ni los egos", asegura el psicólogo del Cisneros. Esa filosofía sigue presente en los vestuarios actuales. El escenario es incomparable, pero algunos de los mecanismos psicológicos utilizados para enfrentarse a la incertidumbre tiene un punto de encuentro: reducir lo incontrolable, repartir responsabilidades y concentrarse en aquello sobre lo que todavía se puede actuar. Quince jugadores avanzan hacia el mismo objetivo y cada uno depende de lo que haga quien tiene al lado. El esfuerzo individual pierde buena parte de su sentido si no repercute sobre el colectivo. Y esa interdependencia termina creando vínculos que, según Antonio, trascienden incluso el compañerismo: "Aquí te sacrificas y te rompes los cuernos por tu compañero. Eso derriba una barrera que va más allá del compañerismo. Hablamos de fraternidad, de amistad e incluso de familia". Convertir un grupo de buenos deportistas en un verdadero equipo implica precisamente abandonar parte de esa individualidad. "Hay que destruir el ego y pensar en quien tienes al lado. Lo que haces, lo haces también por él, porque si tú fallas, el perjudicado es tu compañero y todos los que te rodean", relata. El compromiso, por tanto, no empieza cuando el árbitro señala el inicio del partido. Descansar, entrenar, alimentarse o llegar preparado también afecta al compañero. La exigencia deja de ser exclusivamente personal para convertirse en una responsabilidad colectiva. "La clave de un verdadero equipo llega cuando no tienes que esperar a que nadie venga a exigirte más. Sabes que tu exigencia se transformará en valor para el equipo y que la falta de ella también terminará perjudicándolo". Cada temporada, Antonio pide a sus jugadores de Cisneros que escriban de forma anónima cuál será su compromiso con el equipo. Entre aquellos papeles conserva uno: "Me comprometo a poner mi cuerpo a disposición del equipo". Quizá pocas frases expliquen mejor un deporte construido alrededor del compañero. La psicología deportiva trabaja precisamente sobre muchos de esos mecanismos. No como una herramienta a la que acudir únicamente cuando aparece un problema, sino como una capacidad más que puede entrenarse. Para Antonio es fundamental "cambiar el enfoque. En lugar de tratar de resolver un déficit que tienen los jugadores, lo que hacemos es potenciar sus habilidades. Igual que entrenamos el físico, tenemos que entrenar la concentración, la gestión de la frustración y el lenguaje con el que nos hablamos". Y para hacerlo, Antonio intenta reducir aquello que un deportista no puede controlar. Un jugador le regaló una definición que desde entonces utiliza en su trabajo: "Antonio, un partido de rugby no es un partido de 80 minutos; son 80 partidos de un minuto". El principio es sencillo. No pensar en todo lo que queda. Ni siquiera en todo lo que acaba de ocurrir. Solo en aquello que viene inmediatamente después. "Nos centramos en el siguiente minuto, después en el siguiente y luego en el siguiente. Reducimos todo lo abstracto de un partido completo y empezamos a controlar aquello que tenemos delante". También se entrena lo inesperado. Antonio lo llama entrenar la incertidumbre. En ocasiones, cuando los jugadores creen haber terminado una sesión, acuerda con los preparadores físicos añadir una tarea más. No importa tanto ese esfuerzo añadido como la respuesta ante un escenario que no estaba previsto. "Trabajamos qué hacer cuando las cosas se tuercen. Así se acostumbran a que el valor y el rendimiento no los decida un número y a seguir dando un poco más incluso cuando parece que todo está perdido", explica. Hace dos años, Cisneros perdía por 14 puntos a falta de siete minutos en unos cuartos de final disputados en Burgos. Terminó ganando por uno. Para Antonio, aquella remontada tuvo mucho que ver con haber aprendido previamente a seguir compitiendo cuando el resultado invitaba a pensar lo contrario. La llegada de Antonio de Castro al Cisneros se produjo casi por una coincidencia de necesidades. Por aquel entonces, Tobías Cagigal y Daniel Vinuesa buscaban incorporar a un psicólogo deportivo al club, mientras él trataba de encontrar un equipo en el que comenzar a desarrollar esa faceta profesional. Su currículum llegó a sus manos y decidieron apostar por él pese a que, hasta entonces, su experiencia se había limitado al trabajo individual con deportistas y nunca había formado parte de la estructura de un equipo. Una oportunidad que De Castro agradece especialmente; "Sabemos que es un riesgo para todos, pero queremos confiar en ti", recuerda que le dijeron. Y ahí aparece otra de las ideas sobre las que construye su trabajo. El éxito de la psicología deportiva no puede medirse únicamente mirando un marcador. "Yo me centro en objetivos de proceso, no de resultados. El resultado es blanco o negro: ganas o no ganas. El proceso, en cambio, tiene escalas de grises. Incluso sin ganar puedes haber conseguido cosas. Mi objetivo es conseguir deportistas competitivos, no ganadores", señala. Los resultados de Cisneros desde su llegada han acompañado ese proceso: una final de División de Honor en 2025 después de décadas sin alcanzarla, una final de Copa del Rey, una cuarta posición liguera y un tercer puesto en Seven. Pero Antonio invierte la relación causa-efecto. "Creo que el trabajo está bien hecho, no por el resultado, sino por lo que se ha conseguido en los jugadores, porque eso es lo que después les ha llevado a esos resultados". La fortaleza mental tampoco significa eliminar la frustración, el miedo o la incomodidad. Significa aprender a competir también cuando aparecen. Antonio no deja de aprender de sus compañeros, entre ellos nombra a Gastón, uno de los entrenadores del equipo que dice: "Hay que aprender a estar cómodos en la incomodidad". Esa preparación adquiere otra dimensión cuando el problema deja de ser un resultado y aparece una lesión. Entonces el deportista puede enfrentarse no solo a la imposibilidad de competir, sino a algo más profundo: descubrir cuánto de su identidad había construido alrededor del deporte. Antonio recurre a una metáfora. "Muchas veces el deportista tiene toda su vida estructurada alrededor del deporte. Es como un sistema solar: tienes un sol y todos los planetas giran a su alrededor. Si tu único sol es el deporte y un día se apaga por una lesión, toda tu vida se desmorona. Lo que intentamos es construir nuevos soles para que, cuando uno se apague, puedas seguir obteniendo energía de otros", Por eso distingue poco entre la psicología destinada al rendimiento y la relacionada con el bienestar del deportista. Una termina repercutiendo inevitablemente sobre la otra. "Si ofrecemos herramientas para mejorar la estabilidad emocional, la toma de decisiones o la gestión emocional fuera del campo, eso se va a ver reflejado dentro. Y ocurre también al revés". En Cisneros, además, su trabajo no queda reservado al primer equipo. Antonio interviene de manera transversal en la estructura: con quien solicita su ayuda, pero también con aquellos jugadores en los que detecta que puede resultar necesaria. Porque cuando todos ellos se encuentran, explica, ocurre algo particular. Uno puede ser matemático; otro, ingeniero; otro, analista financiero; otro, profesor. Durante unas horas esas identidades individuales conviven con otra que pertenece a todos. "Cuando todos se juntan, todo aquello adquiere una identidad nueva", asegura. Y quizá esa sea también la mejor manera de regresar al lugar donde comenzó esta historia. Antonio tenía 12 años cuando su madre le habló por primera vez de ¡Viven! y vio la película sobre la tragedia de los Andes. Algo de aquella historia se quedó con él. "No podía dejar de verla. Sentía la necesidad de leer más, de saber más, de profundizar más", recuerda. Durante años estudió lo sucedido. Leyó sobre sus protagonistas y, mucho después, acabó conociendo a algunos de quienes habían regresado de aquella montaña. En ese camino apareció Pablo Vierci, escritor uruguayo y autor de La sociedad de la nieve, con quien entabló una estrecha amistad. Vierci terminó abriéndole la puerta que durante años había observado desde lejos: la de los supervivientes. Y entonces apareció Roberto Canessa. El mismo joven que había sobrevivido en los Andes y que, junto a Fernando Parrado, atravesó la cordillera en busca de ayuda supo años después que aquel niño fascinado por su historia se había convertido en psicólogo deportivo. Canessa puso a Antonio en contacto con Tomás Fonseca, entrenador del Old Christians, para colaborar en la preparación psicológica del equipo. El mismo club del que procedían muchos de los jóvenes que viajaban en aquel avión en octubre de 1972. Hoy, desde Madrid, Antonio trabaja telemáticamente con el conjunto uruguayo. Durante años estudió aquella historia desde los libros. Después conoció a quienes consiguieron regresar de la montaña. Más de medio siglo después del accidente, trabaja con el club alrededor del cual comenzó todo. El rugby volvió a unir los dos extremos de la historia. "Para mí, el círculo se acaba de cerrar".

articles.title: Lewis Ludlow: Gloucester flanker says losing captaincy last year was 'brutal'
articles.summary: Gloucester's Lewis Ludlow on losing the captaincy last season, his two England caps, and chasing a record in his upcoming testimonial season.
articles.body:
Gloucester flanker Lewis Ludlow says it was "brutal" to lose the club captaincy last August and he would "take it back tomorrow" if offered.

Ludlow has played more than 250 games for the Cherry and Whites and his time as skipper between 2020 and 2025 makes him the longest-serving captain in the club's history.

However, the 31-year-old was replaced by Tomos Williams in the role for the 2025-26 season, although the Welshman signed for Saracens this summer.

"It was brutal," Ludlow told BBC Radio Gloucestershire about being told he was no longer captain.

"I didn't change personally, but it takes some getting used to."

Singleton nearing end of rehab but leaves Gloucester

Gloucester decide against Villa Park return

Champions Saints host Newcastle on opening weekend

Ludlow was speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire for an hour-long interview special as he prepares for his testimonial season at the Prem club.

While he felt the captaincy change was coming, he was still surprised when the conversation happened during pre-season.

"I'd kind of prepared myself for it because it was always going to happen at some point," he said.

"I didn't think it would be that timing but it was and I felt like the only thing I could do then was worry about my rugby and be the best bloke I could be to help Tommy [Williams].

"From what people have said, I did that. I'm probably prouder of that than anything. I've been in changing rooms where people aren't that bloke and it makes it very difficult. But I didn't want that to be the case."

Despite the change Ludlow said team-mates still often referred to him as 'Skip' and referees would seek him out post-match as they were so used to him being captain.

However, he believes he and Williams created a working relationship that still allowed Ludlow to use his authority in the team.

"We did as good as we could in terms of balancing him being captain, me still leading where I could and trying to be as effective as possible," Ludlow said.

'Always be grateful' to have captained England

Ludlow has also worn the captain's armband for England, although remarkably the two games in which he captained his country in 2021 remain the only two he has ever played at international level.

He was named captain by then head coach Eddie Jones for matches against the USA and Canada at a time when an array of players were away on Lions duty and Jones was looking to widen his squad before the 2023 World Cup.

Ludlow became just the fifth player to ever captain England on his debut.

But after receiving a red card against Canada, and a subsequent four-game ban for foul play, he never played for England again even though Jones wrote a letter of praise for his disciplinary committee.

"It was possibly the nicest thing anyone's ever written about me and he [Jones] explained why he picked me as captain, the leadership skills I've shown and how he'd been to watch all the games during the season," Ludlow said.

"It was what I was doing in the warm-ups, what I was doing in the huddles, what I was doing post-game, which is why he wanted to make me the captain."

Ludlow was called into training camps in the period that followed but said he has no regrets about never pulling on a Red Rose shirt again.

"When I finished that summer I'd never been fitter, I'd never been stronger," he said.

"We played some class rugby in those two games and I got to become the fifth person to captain my country ever on debut and for that I'll always be grateful."

The 2026-27 season will be Ludlow's 14th at Gloucester after coming through their academy and he has his sights on surpassing Nick Wood's all-time club record of 277 appearances in the professional era.

Ludlow said his body feels "really good" going into the new season after his 2025-26 campaign was disrupted by persistent injuries to his hand and wrist that meant undergoing surgery in April.

The surgery, which fused joints in his thumb on his right hand, means he finally feels pain free for the first time in five years, even though he will continue to wear a cast during games.

Because of the pain he sometimes could not pick up his young son, or even pick up everyday items like a kettle or saucepan.

"To be able to just do normal everyday tasks without things hurting as much as they did, it's quite strange really, but it was a nice feeling," he said.

Ludlow has two clear goals for his testimonial season, which has events scheduled over the next 12 months.

The first is to raise money for two charities: 4Ed, which was set up by his friend and former team-mate Ed Slater after he was diagnosed with motor neurone disease, and the National Foundation for Retired Service Animals. The second is to break Wood's record.

"I want to give as much to those two charities as possible to be able to make a statement of 'this is what I've given these guys' and be able to list off to fans where it's gone and how it's done and how it's worked out," he said.

"And then during the season I need 13 games. It'd be an amazing testimonial season to break Woody's record.

"I know when and where it should be, but there's a long way to go before then."

articles.title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Springboks make one change to squad for third Test with Kurt-Lee Arendse replacing Damian Willemse
articles.summary: South Africa head coach has been forced into one change ahead of the third Test against New Zealand on Saturday; the four-match series is level at 1-1; watch every minute of New Zealand's tour of South Africa exclusively live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
The change comes due to Damien Willemse being sidelined through injury. That means Cheslin Kolbe ‌moves from winger to fullback and Kurt-Lee Arendse comes into ​the squad to take the place of Kolbe on the edge.

Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu will once again start at fly-half with Manie Libbok on the bench. Handre Pollard continues to be ruled out due to a calf problem.

Captain Siya Kolisi starts the third Test after his return from a hamstring issue and makes up the back row with Pieter-Steph du Toit and Jasper Wiese.

Meanwhile, Eben Etzebeth will make his 145th appearance for the Springboks at lock, extending his record as the most capped South Africa player ever.

The front row is then make up of hooker Malcolm Marx and props Ox ⁠Nche and Wilco Louw.

"It was ​always our plan to have a little more continuity ​in player combinations for this series and we thought that the ​players who did the job for us last week really showed composure ⁠and did well to stick to the plan and what we wanted to achieve last week," said Erasmus.

South Africa roared back into Rugby's Greatest Rivalry as returning captain Kolisi marked his comeback with a try in a thrilling 33-26 victory over New Zealand in Cape Town, levelling the four-Test series at 1-1.
